scenes.say: Why is there a point inside every Gaussian splat? And what happens if that point becomes a line?

scenes.headline: How a Gaussian splat becomes a strand
scenes.sub: Five 3D reconstruction papers, explained from the mechanism up
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Mirabel! Five 3D reconstruction papers from this week. We'll go deep on two of them.

scenes.title: A point was a choice
scenes.sub: Spaghetti Splatting turns the point into a segment
scenes.say: Chapter one. A point was a choice.

steps.term: Convolve: blur one shape by another
steps.say: A three D Gaussian is a point, blurred by a smooth kernel. That makes it something a renderer can differentiate.
So a splat has two knobs: the kernel, and the thing being blurred. Swap the point for a segment, or a curve, and you get these soft tubes.

scenes.text: A 3D Gaussian is a point convolved with a smooth kernel. Spaghetti Splatting convolves a line segment instead, and keeps a closed form.
scenes.say: A Gaussian is a point blurred by a kernel. Spaghetti Splatting blurs a line segment instead, and stays in closed form.

scenes.title: From a segment to a pixel

steps.say: Take a segment, two endpoints. Every point along it adds a Gaussian, and together they make a soft tube. Set the endpoints equal and it is an ordinary splat.
Along a camera ray, that tube integrates to two error functions. No sampling.
steps.term: Ray integral: how much density a camera ray crosses

steps.say: Each segment gets an opacity per pixel, composited like ordinary splats.
Cut a segment in half, and the two halves composite to exactly the parent. The image does not move, so training can split freely.

parts.note: the segment before the point closest to the ray
parts.say: Find the point on the segment closest to the ray. One error function counts the part of the segment before it.

parts.note: the part after it; past an end, it fades
parts.say: The other counts the part after. A ray passing beyond an end drives one negative, and the contribution fades.

parts.note: a triangle would need Owen's T; a segment needs only erf
parts.say: A triangle would need a much harder function here. A segment needs only erf, which is why the authors stop at curves.

left.title: Gaussian points
left.say: With points, a thin strand needs a Gaussian every two kernel widths, or it beads.

right.title: One segment
right.say: A segment draws it with one primitive, and bends with a simulator.

legend: Cut at the midpoint, slide apart, slide back

steps.say: The article's toy draws one line with Gaussian points. Five points, and the density ripples by seventeen percent.
Six points, two kernel widths apart: two point nine percent.
Seven: zero point three. A thin strand needs a point every two widths.
One segment, convolved with the same kernel: one primitive, and no ripple at all.
Cut it in half, slide the halves apart and back. The halves sum to the parent exactly, so the image does not move, and training can split freely.
On a real room, the point version draws the bicycle spokes as scattered dots.
The segments run along the spokes and edges, like pencil strokes.

scenes.title: Hair, PSNR in dB
scenes.note: eight GeomHair styles plus one curly model
scenes.say: On rooms it ties ordinary splatting, as a superset should. On hair it wins outright, by two point seven decibels, with no hair prior.

scenes.title: One scale is not enough
scenes.sub: AffineGS aligns monocular depth surface by surface
scenes.say: Chapter two. One scale is not enough.

steps.term: Monocular depth: relative depth from one image
steps.say: Splats reconstruct geometry badly, so people add a depth network as a prior. Its depth is relative, so it is aligned with one global scale and shift. That leaves forty-one percent of pixels off.
Give each of three regions its own scale and shift, and eighty-four point nine percent fit.
With five, ninety-two point seven.
The paper's scatter shows why. Predicted against true disparity falls on three different lines, one per surface.
So AffineGS estimates a scale field that follows those surfaces.

scenes.title: AffineGS: a scale and shift per pixel

parts.note: relative depth from a monocular network
a scale that varies across the image
parts.say: The scale changes from surface to surface, not one number per image.

parts.note: a shift, smoothed by a guided filter
parts.say: A guided filter keeps both fields smooth within a surface. Without it they would copy the render.

scenes.say: AffineGS models the relation per pixel.

scenes.title: Mesh F-score on MuSHRoom
scenes.note: The global-fit baseline was built by the authors
scenes.say: On a benchmark of indoor rooms, meshes score point seven one, against point two eight for a global fit the authors built themselves.

items.say: Gaussian Grids hangs a feature grid on every 2D Gaussian.

items.say: And one from Meta lets a stereo pair set metric depth, under a small decoder.

scenes.say: Three more papers this week, briefly.

steps.say: Here is Click3R. A person clicks the same corner of a toaster in two photos.
The base model alone splits the toaster in two. With one click, it is a single object.

scenes.title: Where the headlines thin
scenes.say: The article checked each claim against its own tables.

items.say: Spaghetti's long connected strands average three and a half segments, and the code is not out yet.
AffineGS initialises from sensor depth points, and tunes its filter scene by scene.
And Gaussian Grids' point one bits per pixel is about point one three, by its own file sizes.
